citations.quote: For a connected regular link projection on $S^2$ with at least one crossing and either checkerboard coloring, both Tait graphs are connected.

For a link projection on $S^2$, a **checkerboard coloring** assigns one of two colors to each complementary region so that regions sharing an edge have different colors. Given such a coloring, the **black Tait graph** has one vertex for each black region and one edge for each crossing joining the two opposite black sectors at that crossing. The **white Tait graph** is defined by interchanging black and white. Loops and parallel edges are allowed.

Assume full AC. Let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth embedded surface with nonempty boundary, possibly nonorientable, with a supplied finite smooth disk-and-band presentation. The ambient three-sphere has its standard orientation. For oriented integral multicurves $a,b\subset\operatorname{int}F$, let $\tau b$ be the cycle consisting of the two small normal pushes over $b$, oriented by projection to $b$. For a one-sided circle this is one circle mapping with degree two, rather than a choice of a single normal direction. Then
$B_F([a],[b])=\operatorname{lk}(a,\tau b)$ defines a well-defined symmetric integral bilinear pairing on $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, independently of representatives and sufficiently small normal pushes. Every integral homology class has an oriented multicurve representative, permitting integer coefficients. The pairing extends to rational homology, with quadratic form $q_F(x)=B_F(x,x)$ satisfying the normal-transfer linking identity.

For an embedded compact subsurface $A\subset F$ with such a finite presentation, the pairing on $A$ is the pullback of $B_F$ under inclusion. If $F$ is oriented and its boundary is one knot, its pairing has matrix $V+V^T$ in any integral basis, where $V$ is the positive-push Seifert matrix. Orientation-preserving ambient isotopies transport the pairing.

Let $D$ be a connected alternating regular link diagram on an oriented projection sphere. Choose either checkerboard color. Put a disk in each region of that color and join the opposite colored sectors at every crossing by a half-twisted band, with the twist chosen so that the boundary follows the over-under diagram. After rounding corners these disks and bands form a compact connected embedded spanning surface $F$ for the represented link. If $D$ has crossings, let $G$ be the corresponding Tait graph and orient its edges arbitrarily. Under the retraction of $F$ onto $G$, write a rational homology class as the unique graph cycle $a=\sum_{e\in E(G)}a_e e$. There is a single sign $\epsilon\in\{1,-1\}$ such that
$$q(a)=\epsilon\sum_{e\in E(G)}a_e^2=\operatorname{lk}(c,\tau c)$$
for every oriented rational multicurve $c$ representing $a$, where $\tau c$ is its normal transfer. Thus $q$ is positive definite or negative definite on $H_1(F;\mathbb Q)$. For a crossingless connected diagram, use either spanning disk and the zero-dimensional definite form.

For every CW complex $X$, abelian group $G$, and $n\geq0$, the cellular complex has an
isomorphism $H_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X;G)\cong H_n(X;G)$, natural with respect to
cellular maps.

For $n\ge1$, $\widetilde H_k(S^n;G)$ is $G$ for $k=n$ and $0$ otherwise.
For $S^0$, $\widetilde H_0(S^0;G)\cong G$ and all other reduced groups vanish.
Thus $H_0(S^n;G)\cong G$ for $n\ge1$, whereas
$H_0(S^0;G)\cong G\oplus G$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For Jordan curves $C$ and $C'$ in $\mathbb R^2$,
every homeomorphism $h:C\to C'$ extends to a homeomorphism
$H:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$ that maps the bounded and unbounded complementary
components of $C$ to the corresponding components of $C'$. In particular each
closed bounded Jordan region is a closed $2$-disk.

derivations.claim: A crossingless connected diagram is a single circle and is alternating vacuously. Otherwise put a vertex in each black disk and a core through each black band. This embeds the connected black Tait graph $G$ in the sphere, with white regions its disk faces. One can see the disk-face assertion by thickening the connected graph: each boundary circle bounds, on its side away from that connected neighborhood, a disk; those disjoint disks fill the complement. Equivalently these are the original checkerboard regions shrunk across the crossing strips. Orient the edges of $G$ and identify their rational chain space with $E=\mathbb Q^m$, with its coordinate Euclidean inner product. Let $C=\ker\partial_1$ be its cycle space. The black surface retracts onto $G$, so its first rational homology is exactly $C$.

Draw the white dual graph, orienting each dual edge by positive intersection with its primal edge. Its cycles, expressed in these same edge coordinates, form precisely $C^\perp$. Indeed the dual is a cellular graph on the sphere. By [F4], every dual cycle is the boundary of a rational sum of its faces. These faces correspond to the primal vertices; their oriented boundary vectors, in crossing coordinates, are the signed incidence rows of $\partial_1$, up to one common orientation convention. Thus the dual cycle space is $\operatorname{im}\partial_1^T$. Finite rational elimination gives $E=\ker\partial_1\oplus\operatorname{im}\partial_1^T$ orthogonally: their intersection is zero since $\langle\partial_1^T u,x\rangle=\langle u,\partial_1x\rangle$, and the rank-nullity dimensions sum to $m$. Hence the white first homology is the required orthogonal complement, including primal loops and bridges.

At crossing $e$ denote the black band's planar half-turn incidence by $\epsilon_e\in\{1,-1\}$. The white band has incidence $-\epsilon_e$: in the same four-sector crossing chart its attaching sectors are the other two, so its normal half-turn runs in the opposite direction while its boundary retains the same overpassing branch. For any graph cycle, clear denominators and run signed parallel strands through each band, joining them in the disk cores. For an original strand and a transferred strand a half-turn gives two mixed crossings of the same incidence sign, one from each normal side; the linking count is half their signed sum. Reversing either strand reverses that contribution. Summing the ordered strand pairs therefore gives $\epsilon_e a_e^2$ at the black band. On the planar disk cores the two normal sides give opposite contributions, including crossings of the joining arcs; these cancel. This is the local strip computation of [F3], now retaining each band's own sign. Restore rational coefficients to obtain $q_B(a)=\sum_e\epsilon_e a_e^2$ on $C$ and $q_W(b)=-\sum_e\epsilon_e b_e^2$ on $C^\perp$. No alternation has been assumed in this computation.

Choose $\sigma=1$ if $q_B$ is positive and $q_W$ negative, and $\sigma=-1$ otherwise. Then $Q(x)=\sum_e\sigma\epsilon_e x_e^2$ is positive on every nonzero rational vector in either $C$ or $C^\perp$. Suppose some coefficient $\sigma\epsilon_e$ is negative. Let $N$ be the coordinate subspace of all such edges and $P_N$ its orthogonal projection. For a nonzero vector $u$ in either subspace, positivity says $\|P_Nu\|^2<\|u\|^2/2$. Decompose the corresponding negative unit coordinate vector as $e=c+d$, with $c\in C$, $d\in C^\perp$; the decomposition is rational by finite elimination. At least one summand is nonzero. The triangle and two-term Cauchy inequalities give $1=\|P_Ne\|\le\|P_Nc\|+\|P_Nd\|<(\|c\|+\|d\|)/\sqrt2\le\sqrt{\|c\|^2+\|d\|^2}=1$, a contradiction. Thus every $\epsilon_e=\sigma$. This argument also applies when one cycle space is zero.

Finally check alternation along any projection edge. The chosen-color sector lies on opposite local sides when that edge is read outward from its two crossing ends. In a half-twist chart, changing that sector side reverses its incidence sign, and switching the visited strand between over and under also reverses it. Therefore equal incidence signs at the two ends hold exactly when those two crossing visits have opposite over-under status. Step 4.1 supplies equal signs at every pair of ends, including when an edge returns to the same crossing. Successive visits along every link component consequently switch over and under. This is alternation by definition, with no assertion about reducedness or primeness.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement allows zero first homology and the crossingless circle; its zero-dimensional pairings and identity local construction are explicit.
The Statement includes a one-component knot and a single crossing; the graph proof includes loops and bridges.
The Statement retains disconnected initial surfaces and nonorientability; all required strict definiteness assumptions are explicit, including zero-dimensional forms.
The Statement transports boundary orientations; the Proof retains distinct endpoints and supplied radial collars where used.
The Statement assumes full AC and its exact inherited uses are recorded in axiom_use.

axioms.use: Full AC is inherited from the normal-transfer linking interface. The graph decomposition, band calculation and definiteness argument are finite rational constructions.

Assume full AC. Let $F_0,F_1\subset S^3$ be compact smooth embedded surfaces with the same nonempty boundary link $L$, with no closed components and with supplied radial collars around $L$. Suppose their entire intersection is $L$ together with $n$ pairwise disjoint smooth arcs $A_1,\ldots,A_n$ whose distinct endpoints lie on $L$. Each arc is the isolated radial extension of a proper transverse common arc in the link exterior; the two boundary curves on the surrounding tori cross transversely at its endpoints, with equal ordered intersection signs when the tori are oriented outward toward the exterior. Thus every arc is standard. No intersection circles occur.

Write $b_i=\operatorname{rank}H_1(F_i;\mathbb Z)$ and suppose $c(F_0)=c(F_1)=p$ and $n=b_0+b_1$. There is a continuous surjection $q:S^3\to S^3$ whose only nonsingleton fibers are exactly the arcs $A_j$, supported in any prescribed disjoint neighborhoods of those arcs. Its image $S=q(F_0\cup F_1)$ is a disjoint union of exactly $p$ locally flat embedded topological two-spheres. Each component of $S$ contains the images of exactly one component of each $F_i$. The conclusion includes $n=0$ and allows nonorientable or disconnected spanning surfaces. It does not assert smoothness of these quotient spheres or reconstruct a link diagram.

Assume full AC. Take a surface pair and its standard finite intersection arcs satisfying the hypotheses of the balanced-span smooth sphere quotient: the common boundary link is nonempty, there are no closed surface components or intersection circles, both surfaces have $p$ components, and the number of standard arcs equals the sum of their first Betti numbers. Let $Q$ be a continuous ambient surjection with exactly those arc fibers, whose surface image $S=Q(F_0\cup F_1)$ is a disjoint union of $p$ spheres and whose every sphere contains the images of exactly one component of each surface. In particular one may take the smooth sphere quotient constructed there.

Then $G=Q(L)\subset S$ is a finite topologically embedded graph, connected on each sphere. Its vertices are the distinct points $Q(A_j)$, each of valence four; components without vertices are circles. At each vertex there is a supplied topological disk chart with four radial graph arms, with the sectors from $Q(F_0)$ and $Q(F_1)$ alternating cyclically. Away from vertices the graph has an ordinary line chart, and each component of $S\setminus G$ belongs to exactly one of the two surface images. This is a topological marked graph assertion; it does not assert that the graph is smooth or specify overcrossings.

Assume full AC. Let two compact smooth embedded surfaces span the same smooth link with supplied radial collars. Let $A$ be an isolated smooth radial extension of a proper transverse common arc in the link exterior, with transverse boundary-curve crossings and equal ordered endpoint signs on the tori oriented outward toward the exterior.

There is a smooth ambient coordinate chart near $A$, with $A=[-1,1]\times\{0,0\}$, in which the first surface is $z=0$, $-1\le x\le1$, and the local link is the two end lines $x=\pm1,z=0$. An ambient topological isotopy supported in this chart, fixing that first surface and the literal link pointwise, carries the second surface in a smaller normal cylinder to
$$\{(x,R\cos\theta(x),R\sin\theta(x)):-1\le x\le1,\ |R|<r_0\},$$
where $\theta(x)=\pi(x+1)/2$ or $\pi(1-x)/2$. It fixes the common arc pointwise and introduces no other identifications. No differentiability of the ambient isotopy at the two end faces or at the common axis is asserted. This is a local surface-pair normal form, without a diagram reconstruction conclusion.

Let $\alpha:[-1,1]\hookrightarrow S^3$ be a smooth embedding with nonvanishing derivative, smooth in boundary charts at both endpoints, and let $U$ be an open neighborhood of its image $A$. Then there is a continuous surjection $q:S^3\to S^3$, fixed on $S^3\setminus U$, whose only non-singleton fiber is $A$. In particular the quotient space $S^3/A$, obtained by identifying exactly the points of $A$ to one point, is homeomorphic to $S^3$.

Moreover there is a continuous family $Q:S^3\times[0,1]\to S^3$ with $Q_0=\operatorname{id}$ and $Q_1=q$, fixed on $S^3\setminus U$, such that every $Q_t$ for $0\le t<1$ is a homeomorphism. Every closed parameter interval $[0,t_0]$ with $t_0<1$ therefore gives an ambient topological isotopy. The assertion concerns a topological quotient; it does not assert that the terminal map is a diffeomorphism or that an arbitrary surface containing the arc becomes a surface after collapse.

Take four rectangles $P_j=[0,1]_t\times[0,1]_r$, $j\in\{0,1,2,3\}$. Identify their edges $r=0$ pointwise in the $t$ coordinate to a common arc $A$. At each end $t=e$, $e\in\{0,1\}$, also identify the radial edges pointwise in $r$ by a matching $\mu_e$, where each $\mu_e$ is one of $M=(01)(23)$ and $N=(03)(12)$. Let $K$ be this finite quotient complex, and let $C$ be the image of the four outer edges $r=1$.

If the two end matchings differ, then $K/A$ is a closed topological disk whose boundary is exactly the image of $C$, and the collapsed arc is an interior point of that disk. If the two end matchings agree, then $K/A$ is two closed disks joined at their interior centers, so it is not a topological two-manifold at the collapsed point. Explicitly, $K/A$ is the cone on the graph $C$; the latter is one four-edge circle for distinct matchings and two disjoint two-edge circles for equal matchings.

Consequently, if a finite Hausdorff two-dimensional cell complex is already a topological two-manifold away from finitely many disjoint arc subcomplexes, with neighborhoods modeled by the interiors $r<1$ of these four-page models with distinct end matchings, collapsing those arcs gives a topological two-manifold. No boundary is created at a collapsed point. Collapsing any finite disjoint arc subcomplexes preserves the Euler characteristic, whether or not the local end matchings differ. These are intrinsic topological conclusions; an ambient embedding or local flatness needs separate data.

Assume full AC. Let $S$ be a compact embedded topological surface in an oriented smooth three-manifold. Suppose it is smooth outside finitely many pairwise disjoint smoothly parametrized seam circles or compact seam arcs, all contained in the interior of $S$. Near each seam it is the union of two supplied smooth embedded half-surfaces meeting precisely in that seam; their inward transverse tangent rays are distinct at every seam point. For an arc, both half-surfaces extend smoothly slightly past its end parameters, and the union $S$ is already smooth on a neighborhood of the two ends. Let $K\subset S$ be a compact set on a neighborhood of which $S$ is smooth.

In any prescribed neighborhood of the nonsmooth locus there is an ambient homeomorphism, supported in that neighborhood and fixed on a neighborhood of $K$, carrying $S$ to a smooth embedded surface. It can be joined to the identity through ambient homeomorphisms with those same support and fixed-set properties. This preserves the surface's homeomorphism type. Distinct rays may be opposite, in which case the surface may already be smooth; they must not coincide. No triangulation or general locally-flat surface smoothing theorem is assumed.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. A compact $C^2$ surface, with regular $C^2$ boundary allowed, is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to a compact smooth surface with smooth boundary. For a compact cooriented embedded surface in a smooth three-manifold, the diffeomorphism can be obtained by arbitrarily small local ambient displacements. This also applies to a compact intrinsic subsurface of a $C^2$ leaf: compactness is in the leaf topology, and its boundary is regular in that topology.

A connected oriented closed such surface with Euler characteristic zero is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $T^2$. A compact regular surface region homeomorphic to a closed disk is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $D^2$, and any prescribed $C^2$ diffeomorphism of its boundary circle can be realized by the disk parametrization.

Two disjoint regular closed disk regions in a $C^2$ sphere can simultaneously be carried to the standard two disk windows by a $C^2$ diffeomorphism, with compatible prescribed boundary parametrizations. A $C^2$ scalar function defined on a neighborhood of a compact set in $\mathbb R^2$ admits smooth approximations uniformly with its derivatives through order two on that compact set.

Finally let $L$ be a $C^2$ surface and $u:D^2\to L$ an **intrinsically continuous** map which is $C^2$ on an open boundary collar. On any smaller closed boundary collar contained in that open collar, $u$ has arbitrarily close $C^2$ approximations agreeing with $u$ on a neighborhood of the smaller collar, and a homotopy to each approximation fixed there. Closeness is uniform for any fixed compatible metric on $L$. No injectivity or immersion of the cap map is required.

Let $P$ be a compact smooth $k$-manifold with boundary, let $N$ be a Hausdorff smooth $n$-manifold without boundary, and let $f:P\times[0,1]\to N$ be jointly smooth with every $f_t$ a smooth embedding. Suppose the family is stationary on neighborhoods of both time endpoints. For every open neighborhood $W$ of its compact track $f(P\times[0,1])$, there is a jointly smooth isotopy $H_t:N\to N$ of diffeomorphisms with $H_0=\operatorname{id}$ and $H_t\circ f_0=f_t$, supported in a fixed compact subset of $W$ and stationary near its time endpoints. No choice axiom is assumed. The empty source and zero-dimensional source are allowed.

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$. For each $p\in M$, let
$\gamma_p:I_p\to M$ be the maximal integral curve through $p$, and set

$$ \mathcal D:=\{(t,p)\in\mathbb R\times M:t\in I_p\}, \qquad \Phi(t,p):=\gamma_p(t). $$

Then $\mathcal D$ is open in $\mathbb R\times M$, each fibre $\mathcal D_p$ is
an interval containing $0$, the map $\Phi:\mathcal D\to M$ is smooth, and
$\Phi$ is the unique maximal local flow generated by $X$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

Assume AC. For $n\ge1$, the image $K$ of a topological embedding $S^{n-1}\hookrightarrow S^n$ has exactly two complementary path components, and $K$ is the common boundary of both.

For an embedding $S^{n-1}\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^n$ with $n\ge2$, there are exactly two complementary components, one bounded and one unbounded, again with common boundary $K$. In the exceptional case $n=1$, an embedded $S^0$ in $\mathbb R$ consists of two points $a<b$ and has three complementary components $(-\infty,a),(a,b),(b,\infty)$, one bounded and two unbounded. No assertion that a component closure is a ball is made. AC is inherited only from Alexander duality.

Assume countable choice. Let $S\subset S^3$ be the image of a smooth embedding of the standard $S^2$. There is a smooth ambient isotopy $H_t:S^3\to S^3$, with $H_0=\operatorname{id}$, such that $H_1(S)$ is the standard equatorial sphere $E$. In particular $S^3\setminus S$ has exactly two components. Their closures $B_+$ and $B_-$ are smoothly embedded standard closed $3$-balls with common boundary $S$. If $D_+$ and $D_-$ denote the standard closed hemispheres bounded by $E$, the labels can be chosen so that the restrictions $H_1:B_\pm\to D_\pm$ are diffeomorphisms with the same boundary restriction $H_1|_S:S\to E$. Thus the ball identifications are compatible on their boundary and on a common two-sided collar of that boundary.
An oriented link $L\subset S^3$ is **split** if a smoothly embedded sphere $S\subset S^3\setminus L$ has link points in both components of $S^3\setminus S$; otherwise $L$ is **nonsplit**.

Assume countable choice. Every connected compact smooth surface $F$ with nonempty boundary has a finite smooth disk-and-band presentation: it is diffeomorphic, respecting its actual boundary parametrization, to finitely many smooth disks with finitely many rectangular bands attached along pairs of disjoint boundary intervals, with compatible corner rounding. Equivalently it has a finite handle decomposition with only zero- and one-handles, all zero-handles first. The assertion allows nonorientable surfaces and twisted bands. For a smoothly embedded surface these data may be transported to the actual surface, so its disk, band and attaching charts are supplied inside that surface, rather than merely as a homotopy type.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. A compact $C^2$ surface, with regular $C^2$ boundary allowed, is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to a compact smooth surface with smooth boundary. For a compact cooriented embedded surface in a smooth three-manifold, the diffeomorphism can be obtained by arbitrarily small local ambient displacements. This also applies to a compact intrinsic subsurface of a $C^2$ leaf: compactness is in the leaf topology, and its boundary is regular in that topology.

A connected oriented closed such surface with Euler characteristic zero is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $T^2$. A compact regular surface region homeomorphic to a closed disk is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $D^2$, and any prescribed $C^2$ diffeomorphism of its boundary circle can be realized by the disk parametrization.

Two disjoint regular closed disk regions in a $C^2$ sphere can simultaneously be carried to the standard two disk windows by a $C^2$ diffeomorphism, with compatible prescribed boundary parametrizations. A $C^2$ scalar function defined on a neighborhood of a compact set in $\mathbb R^2$ admits smooth approximations uniformly with its derivatives through order two on that compact set.

Finally let $L$ be a $C^2$ surface and $u:D^2\to L$ an **intrinsically continuous** map which is $C^2$ on an open boundary collar. On any smaller closed boundary collar contained in that open collar, $u$ has arbitrarily close $C^2$ approximations agreeing with $u$ on a neighborhood of the smaller collar, and a homotopy to each approximation fixed there. Closeness is uniform for any fixed compatible metric on $L$. No injectivity or immersion of the cap map is required.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For Jordan curves $C$ and $C'$ in $\mathbb R^2$,
every homeomorphism $h:C\to C'$ extends to a homeomorphism
$H:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$ that maps the bounded and unbounded complementary
components of $C$ to the corresponding components of $C'$. In particular each
closed bounded Jordan region is a closed $2$-disk.

For a link projection on $S^2$, a **checkerboard coloring** assigns one of two colors to each complementary region so that regions sharing an edge have different colors. Given such a coloring, the **black Tait graph** has one vertex for each black region and one edge for each crossing joining the two opposite black sectors at that crossing. The **white Tait graph** is defined by interchanging black and white. Loops and parallel edges are allowed.

Assume full AC. Let $F\subset S^3$ be a nonempty compact smooth embedded surface, possibly disconnected and nonorientable, every component of which has nonempty boundary. The ambient sphere has its standard orientation. The normal-transfer expression $B_F([a],[b])=\operatorname{lk}(a,\tau b)$ defines a symmetric integral bilinear pairing on the free finite-rank group $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, with rational extension. It restricts on each component to its normal-transfer pairing; for cycles $a,b$ on distinct components its value is $2\operatorname{lk}(a,b)$, which need not vanish.

Suppose an embedded product cylinder $W=[-1,1]\times D^2$ meets $F$ exactly in its two end disks, on distinct components. Replace those disks by the lateral annulus and round the seams to obtain $F'$. There is an integral basis in which $B_{F'}$ has matrix $G\oplus[0]$, where $G$ is the entire matrix of $B_F$, including its cross-component entries. Thus its signature is unchanged. The boundary link and its surface collar remain fixed, so $e(F)=-\sum_i\operatorname{lk}(K_i,K_i')$, computed from boundary normal push-offs, is unchanged as well.

A finite sequence of such tubes exists making $F$ connected. All intermediate surfaces still have the original boundary link and collar, no closed components, and finite smooth disk-and-band presentations on their components. The signature and $e$ are preserved throughout.

Assume full AC. Let $D$ be a connected regular link diagram on an oriented two-sphere, with its two standard smooth checkerboard disk-and-band surfaces $B,W$. If the normal-transfer pairing on $B$ is positive definite and that on $W$ is negative definite, or conversely, then $D$ is alternating. The zero-dimensional form is allowed as either definite sign. No primeness or reducedness assumption is required.

derivations.claim: Apply [F1] to the original pair, obtaining a reference quotient $q_0$, its sphere image and its connected marked graphs. Keep this reference only for their topology and component assignment. Choose disjoint actual arc charts and use [F2] in smaller cylinders. The angular isotopies fix the literal link. Their images of the second surface are still smooth: write the signed normal vector as $t|v(x,t)|(\cos\beta(x,t),\sin\beta(x,t))$, with a smooth angle lift $\beta$ for the nonzero $v$. The formula on that strip is the smooth interpolation from $\beta$ to the ruled angle, with a radius cutoff constant near the axis. It is smooth through $t=0$ and the end faces, has nonzero transverse derivative by monotone normal radius, and is injective by the distinct positive and negative half angles. Outside the supported cylinders it agrees with the old strip. Thus the new pair is smooth, has the same link and the same arc fibers and Betti numbers. In each smaller chart it is exactly the ruled pair with $\theta(x)=\pi(1+\epsilon x)/2$, $\epsilon\in\{1,-1\}$.

In each such chart take a small ellipsoid $B=\{x^2/(1+e^2)+(y^2+z^2)/e^2\le1\}$, with a slightly larger ellipsoid still inside the ruled region. Rotate every normal plane by $-\theta(x)/2$. This rotation is realized by a global smooth ambient isotopy: multiply its angle by a smooth cutoff in the chart, equal to one on the larger ellipsoid, depending smoothly on $x$ and $y^2+z^2$ and zero near the chart boundary. Every time map preserves $x$ and normal radius and is inverted by the opposite angle. It therefore is a smooth diffeomorphism, including at the axis. The local link becomes $\Lambda_y=\{(-\epsilon,t,0):|t|\le d\}$ and $\Lambda_z=\{(\epsilon,0,t):|t|\le d\}$, where $d=e^2/\sqrt{1+e^2}$. Denote the resulting original-link representative by $\widehat L$.

Perform the coordinate arc collapse [F3] in each ellipsoid before this last rotation, and conjugate it by the rotation. Compose the disjoint collapses, obtaining $q$ for the rotated pair, with each ball preserved and its boundary fixed. Its only nonsingleton fibers are the original arc sets, fixed as sets by all the preceding local maps. Conjugating $q_0$ by those preceding ambient homeomorphisms gives another quotient of the rotated pair with precisely the same fibers. The induced map between the two compact Hausdorff quotient targets is a homeomorphism, since each quotient map is continuous and onto. Hence $q$ has the same $p$ sphere components and the same connected marked graphs. Inside each ball, the four actual pages, truncated by the ellipsoid, are parametrized by $x\in[-1,1]$ and normalized normal radius $u\in[0,1]$; opposite end matchings give their cone disk and four radial marked arms by [F3]. Outside the balls its surface image is exactly the rotated original surface union.

Describe its outer page curve in the rotated chart. If $\phi$ is normal angle and $a(\phi)$ its distance from $\pi\mathbb Z$ in $[0,\pi/2]$, put $b(\phi)=\epsilon(4a(\phi)/\pi-1)$. The four edges have angles $\pm\theta/2$ and $\pi\pm\theta/2$, so on every nearby confocal level of parameter $\rho$ their union is $(b(\phi),R_\rho(b(\phi))\cos\phi,R_\rho(b(\phi))\sin\phi)$, where $R_\rho(v)=\rho\sqrt{1-v^2/(1+\rho^2)}$. Replace the cornered function $b$ by the smooth function $b_s(\phi)=-\epsilon\cos(2\phi)$. They have the same four values at angles $0,\pi/2,\pi,3\pi/2$, namely $-\epsilon,\epsilon,-\epsilon,\epsilon$.

Make this replacement on a collar of $\partial B$ by an actual link-fixed ambient topological isotopy. On a confocal level, $x$ runs from $-\sqrt{1+\rho^2}$ to $\sqrt{1+\rho^2}$ at fixed $\phi$. Choose a smooth radial cutoff $\lambda(\rho)$ equal to one on $[e/2,5e/4]$ and zero outside $(e/3,3e/2)$; choose $e$ small enough that these larger levels remain inside the ruled region. Use the increasing piecewise-affine meridian interval map fixing its two poles and taking $b(\phi)$ to $(1-t\lambda)b(\phi)+t\lambda b_s(\phi)$. It and its inverse vary continuously; at a pole continuity follows from its unchanged pole and vanishing normal radius. Extend by the identity off that annular region. At each of the four link directions $b=b_s$, the entire meridian map is the identity, so the literal chords and all of $\widehat L$ remain fixed. Near $\partial B$ the outside surface is now the smooth annulus $x=b_s(\phi)$ on the confocal levels. Each original half-page remains smooth up to its seam: on its closed angular quadrant $b$ is smooth, and the displayed interpolation is smooth in the level and quadrant parameters. The modified seam curve is still the literal smooth link.

In the ball set $R_s(\phi)=R_e(b_s(\phi))$ and $\Omega_s=\{(r\cos\phi,r\sin\phi):0\le r\le R_s(\phi)\}$. This is a smooth star-shaped disk, with $d\le R_s\le e$. Choose a smooth nondecreasing $\zeta:[0,1]\to[0,1]$, zero on $[0,1/2]$ and one on $[3/4,1]$. The graph $P=\{(h(y,z),y,z):(y,z)\in\Omega_s\}$, where $h(r,\phi)=\zeta(r/R_s(\phi))b_s(\phi)$, is smooth, including at the origin where it is identically zero. It is properly embedded in $B$: at radius $r\le R_s$ the allowed absolute $x$ height is $A(r)=\sqrt{1+e^2}\sqrt{1-r^2/e^2}\ge|b_s|\ge|h|$, with strict ball inequality for $r<R_s$. Its boundary is the new smooth page curve. On its boundary collar $h=b_s$, exactly the same parametrized annulus as in step 4.1; hence it glues smoothly to the modified outside surface. Projection of the two literal chords along $x$ onto this disk is $(-\epsilon\zeta(|t|/d),t,0)$ and $(\epsilon\zeta(|t|/d),0,t)$. They are smooth regular curves, meet only at the origin in its flat disk chart, and there cross transversely. Their signed heights are $-\epsilon(1-\zeta)$ and $\epsilon(1-\zeta)$; the two heights are opposite at the crossing, and vanish on the outer collar where projection is the identity.

Replace the collapsed disk in each ball by $P$, leaving the modified outside surface unchanged. This preserves its sphere components and its marked graph topology. Indeed the old disk has the four-page cone chart in step 3.1, transported by the annular homeomorphism. Its four boundary marks are fixed by that homeomorphism. The new disk projects homeomorphically onto $\Omega_s$, with its four marked arms the coordinate radial segments. The prescribed boundary identification extends from the old cone to $\Omega_s$ radially, sending its four marked radii to those four segments; compose with the graph map to $P$. This is a disk homeomorphism agreeing on the entire boundary, so pastes to a homeomorphism of the two global surface-and-graph pairs. Call the new surface $S$ and its projected graph $D$. Thus $S$ has exactly $p$ topological sphere components and $D$ is connected on each, with one vertex for each original arc. Opposite boundary marks are joined by the actual link chords, so these vertices have the correct strand pairing.

Round the remaining seams while keeping the literal link fixed. They are finitely many compact link arcs or circles outside the protected cap collars; their arc ends lie in the smooth annuli from steps 4.1–6.1. Their two inward half-sheet rays are distinct. Outside the normalization cylinders this follows from the original distinct radial collars and smooth rotations. In a normalization cylinder the relative radial collar angle has nonzero derivative at the arc endpoint. In the adapted strip this says $Z=(x-x_{\rm end})t c(x,t)$ with $c(x_{\rm end},0)\ne0$, by applying the two vanishing factors and differentiating the relative collar angle; shrink so $c$ remains nonzero. Therefore the end derivative of the lift $\beta$ in step 1.1 is nonzero and has the same sign as the ruled-angle end derivative, since both angles approach the same endpoint of $[0,\pi]$ from its interior. Their convex interpolation retains that sign, and the derivative of its cutoff is multiplied by $\beta-\theta=0$ at the end. Thus distinct inward rays remain distinct off the original arc endpoints, which are removed inside the balls. Inside an annular quadrant chart the two outgoing angular derivatives have opposite nonzero angular components, so cannot coincide, even when their tangent planes agree. Use [F4]'s seam graph $y=f(s,x)$, with $f(s,0)=0$. Replace its rounding displacement by $\Delta=\mu(s)\chi_0(x)(f^\eta(s,x)-f(s,x)-f^\eta(s,0))$, where $f^\eta$ is the transverse convolution, $\chi_0=1$ near zero, and $\mu=1$ near the nonsmooth locus and is supported away from the protected smooth collars. Near a nonsmooth seam the new graph is $f^\eta(s,x)-f^\eta(s,0)$, hence smooth; all cutoff transitions occur where the old graph is smooth. The error is at most twice the usual convolution error, so shrinking $\eta$ retains [F4]'s positive vertical fiber derivative. Crucially $\Delta(s,0)=0$, and therefore the whole fiber isotopy fixes the seam pointwise. Its support misses the caps and lies where $\widehat L$ is exactly that seam. The resulting $S$ is smooth everywhere, with $\widehat L$ and its diagram projection unchanged.

Each smooth surface component is homeomorphic to $S^2$ by step 6.1. To supply an actual standard smooth sphere parameter, apply [F5]'s finite smooth handle normalization. One zero-disk and one two-disk remain; Euler characteristic two forces zero one-bands. The smooth boundary circle gluing extends across a disk with its transported product collars, giving a smooth standard sphere parameter. The map from $\widehat L$ to $S$ is the identity outside the balls and the projections in step 5.1 inside them. It is smooth at the joins because those projections are the identity on open link collars, is an immersion everywhere, and has precisely the $n$ transverse double points just described, with no other multiple points. Orient its strands from the oriented $\widehat L$. This gives the required regular graphs on the smooth spheres.

Track the two surfaces themselves through the local changes, without replacing their bands by the projection caps. Apart from the smooth rotation in step 2.1, the angular and seam changes restrict to smooth embedding isotopies of either surface, fixed on its boundary link: this was checked for the angular normalization in step 1.1 and for the quadrant pages in step 4.1; in step 7.1 the graph formula is smooth on either closed half-sheet and has zero displacement on the seam. By [F6] each such source isotopy extends smoothly, and its extension fixes the boundary link because the source isotopy does. The resulting surfaces have disk-and-band pieces on the two colors of $S$, with one band neighborhood for each original common arc. To prove that their cut pieces are disks, cut all $n$ arc strips. The interiors of their components correspond bijectively to the colored faces of $D$, by the marked cone charts and the surface-and-graph homeomorphism in step 6.1. A thin smooth regular neighborhood of a connected graph in a sphere has disk complementary regions: every boundary circle bounds a disk on the side missing the connected neighborhood by [F9], and these disks are disjoint and fill its complement. Its Euler count is $-n_a$ for a graph with $n_a$ four-valent vertices, including the circle case, so it has $n_a+2$ boundary circles. Summing gives $n+2p$ cut pieces. Formula [F8] gives $\chi(F_i)=p-b_i$, where $b_i= \operatorname{rank}H_1(F_i;\mathbb Z)$. Cutting each proper arc adds one to Euler characteristic, by restoring its rectangle along two intervals. Hence the sum of the cut-piece Euler characteristics is $2p-b_0-b_1+2n=2p+n$, equal to their number. Each is at most one by [F8], so every cut piece is a disk.

Bring the actual link into an arbitrarily small neighborhood of $S$ by smooth embedding isotopies, without using the arbitrary quotient homeomorphisms on the link. On each chord keep $(y,z)$ fixed and replace its $x$ coordinate by $h(y,z)+k(x-h(y,z))$, with $k$ decreasing smoothly from one to an arbitrarily small positive constant. The displayed chord formulas make this jointly smooth, including the crossing and the stationary outer collars. They remain embeddings: along each branch the nonconstant coordinate is still its parameter, and the only pair of equal projected points is the crossing, where the two nonzero opposite heights remain distinct because $k>0$. They stay inside the convex vertical ball fibers. Extend by the identity on the rest of the link, stationarize time, and apply [F6] to this compact source isotopy. Thus the compressed link is smoothly ambient isotopic to $\widehat L$, hence to the original $L$, and can be made arbitrarily close to its fixed diagram $D$.

Check the bands' actual framing. In a rotated ball, the two band cores are the diagonals $x=0$, with signed core parameter $s$ and normal-plane basis $(x,w)$, where $w$ is the positive quarter-turn of that core in the $(y,z)$ plane. Put $\tau_0=1$, $\tau_1=-1$ for the two colors, $c(s)=1+\lambda(|s|)(\pi/2-1)$, and $z(s)=\zeta(|s|/e)$. Differentiating the ruled strips and their meridian modification at the core gives band width vector $(c(s),-\tau_i\epsilon\pi s/4)$, hence normal vector $N_i=(\tau_i\epsilon\pi s/4,c(s))$. Differentiating the smooth projection disk gives normal $N_S=(1,2\tau_i\epsilon z(s)/s)$, extended smoothly at zero since $z$ vanishes there. Whenever $z>0$, the cutoff in step 4.1 has $\lambda=1$. Therefore $\det(N_S,N_i)=c-\pi z/2\ge0$, while $N_S\cdot N_i=\tau_i\epsilon(\pi s/4+2cz/s)$ has sign $\tau_i\epsilon s$ for $s\ne0$. The relative normal angle lies in $[0,\pi]$, equals zero or $\pi$ on the two attaching collars, and crosses $\pi/2$ only at the center, transversely. Thus each band has exactly one half-turn relative to the sphere framing, with no extra full twists; the two colors have opposite half-turn signs. At the center its positive width direction points toward increasing $x$, so its boundary branch there is exactly the actual overpassing chord specified in step 5.1.

Choose an orientation and positive transverse direction on each sphere. Near the compact cap portions used by the projected chords, choose the transverse field to be $\partial_x$ or $-\partial_x$, according to that positive direction; the graph disk is transverse to this field. Positive transverse fields extend over the rest of the sphere by a finite smooth partition, since the positive normal cone is convex. Its flow gives a common short smooth product collar by [F6]: invertibility holds on the zero section, and compactness excludes collisions in successively shorter strips. With $k$ small enough in step 9.2, the compressed link lies in these disjoint collars and projects exactly to $D$; in the balls its flow segments are the same vertical segments, while outside them the link lies on the sphere. Read the overcrossing data from its positive collar coordinate. This is a simultaneous small-height realization of those oriented diagrams, smoothly equivalent to the original link. If there is only one sphere, apply [F7]'s smooth ambient isotopy to the equator to view it as an ordinary diagram on the oriented projection sphere.

These data identify the smooth checkerboard surfaces by an explicit finite ribbon straightening. In each disk piece choose a smaller round-parameter disk core and disjoint radial spokes to its band windows, all on the colored sphere region; the band cores from step 10.1 complete the embedded Tait graph on $S$. Thin its surface neighborhood in the supplied disk-and-band coordinates: positive radial compressions on disk sectors and positive transverse rescalings on rectangular strips agree after the positive interval interpolations in their attaching collars. They give a smooth embedding isotopy to an arbitrarily narrow ribbon around this graph, carrying the boundary with it. Near each edge core choose smooth tubular coordinates $(s,u,v)$ with $S=\{v=0\}$. Its band is $(s,tV(s)+O(t^2))$. For sufficiently small width, replacing the remainder by $(1-r)O(t^2)$ is an embedding isotopy: projection onto $V(s)$ has strictly positive derivative uniformly, while the coordinate $s$ and disjoint finite tubes exclude all other collisions. Use the disk's product window coordinates to make this replacement fixed on attaching collars. The resulting linear ribbon is determined by its nonzero width field. Interpolate its positive lengths and the relative angle lift in step 10.1 to the standard single half-turn with the same endpoint values, fixing the collars. Choose the target lift on the same side of $\pi/2$ for each sign of $s$; the interpolation retains the unique transverse middle passage and the same overpassing boundary branch. Every intermediate ribbon remains embedded by its fixed $s$ coordinate. On the vertex disks the finite collar maps match the same windows. Thus the endpoint is precisely disks in the chosen-color regions joined by the standard half-twisted crossing bands with the prescribed over-under data. The finite face collars identify their boundary projection with $D$ up to planar isotopy, without changing any crossing or cyclic order. Apply [F6] to these compact smooth source isotopies. This proves that the two checkerboard surfaces have the asserted individual smooth ambient-isotopy classes and transported boundary orientations.

Suppose in addition that the original full pairings are definite with opposite signs. The inclusion of a component is an injection on first homology, since the homology of a finite disjoint union is its direct sum. Its pairing is the restriction of the full pairing by [F10], so the same strict sign holds on each nonzero component class. The individual smooth ambient isotopies of step 11.1 transport these restricted pairings to the two checkerboard surfaces on each projection sphere. Apply [F10]'s converse on that connected diagram. Every diagram is alternating, including the crossingless case. This uses no assumption that the original link or either surface was connected.

Finally suppose $p>1$. The continuous projection of each whole link component lies in one sphere, and every sphere has a nonempty graph, so each carries a nonempty group of complete link components. Compress further so each such group lies in a very thin collar of its sphere. Fix one sphere $S_a$. By [F7] its complement has two sides; some other sphere is on one of those sides, since it is connected and disjoint from $S_a$. Push $S_a$ slightly toward that side, beyond its own thin link collar but still within its collar disjoint from all other spheres and their link groups. This parallel smooth sphere has the group carried by $S_a$ on one side and the selected other group on the other, and misses the entire compressed link. It is a smooth splitting sphere. Pulling it back through the smooth isotopies from step 9.2 gives a splitting sphere for the original link. Consequently nonsplitness forces $p=1$. The empty arc list uses the identity collapse and omits all local ball operations; seam rounding, the component argument and the same conclusion still apply. Nothing in the construction used primeness, so composite nonsplit links are included.

citations.quote:
Assume full AC. Let $F_+,F_-$ be compact smooth embedded spanning surfaces without closed components for the same nonempty oriented link $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_m\subset S^3$. They may be disconnected or nonorientable. Suppose their full normal-transfer pairings are respectively positive and negative definite. Write $f_i(F)$ for the self-linking of $K_i$ with its surface-normal push, oriented compatibly, and put $d_i=f_i(F_+)-f_i(F_-)$. Then $f_i(F_+)\ge0\ge f_i(F_-)$, so $d_i\ge0$, and
$$\sum_i d_i=2\bigl(b_1(F_+)+b_1(F_-)\bigr).$$

The surface $F_+$ can be isotoped fixing its boundary $L$ pointwise so that, in mutually disjoint smooth boundary tubes with coordinates $(s,u,v)$, $s\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$, the actual collar of the fixed comparison surface $F_-$ is the ray of angle zero and that of the changed $F_+$ is the ray of angle $2\pi d_i s+\delta_i$, for a fixed $0<\delta_i<2\pi$. On every sufficiently small tube torus $T_i$, their collar curves then meet transversely in exactly $d_i$ points, all with the same local intersection sign when $d_i>0$. If $d_i=0$ the curves are disjoint. This is the minimum possible geometric intersection count for their slope classes. Orienting $T_i$ by the coordinate order $(s,\theta)$ and both collar curves by increasing $s$, the ordered intersection of the $F_+$ curve with the $F_-$ curve has sign $-1$ at every intersection.

Assume full AC. If $F_0,F_1\subset S^3$ are compact smooth embedded spanning surfaces for the same nonempty link, with no closed components but allowing disconnectedness and nonorientability, then
$$\nu(B_{F_0})+c(F_0)-1=\nu(B_{F_1})+c(F_1)-1.$$
Here $B_F$ is the full rational normal-transfer pairing, including its cross-component entries, $\nu(B_F)$ is the dimension of its kernel, and $c(F)$ is its number of connected components. The quantity is invariant under orientation-preserving ambient isotopy of the boundary link.

Consequently any two such surfaces whose full normal-transfer pairings are nondegenerate have the same number of components. In particular this holds for two definite surfaces of either sign, including opposite signs. If $F_0,F_1$ are definite spanning surfaces for the same link, and proper arcs $\alpha_0\subset F_0$, $\alpha_1\subset F_1$ have the property that their cut surfaces span ambient isotopic links, then $\alpha_0$ separates its surface component if and only if $\alpha_1$ does. This last assertion concerns separation, without asserting an alternating diagram or identifying the number of split components of the link.

Assume full AC. Let $F_+,F_-$ be compact smooth embedded spanning surfaces without closed components for the same nonempty nonsplit link $L\subset S^3$, with respectively positive and negative definite full rational normal-transfer pairings. They may be disconnected and nonorientable. Suppose their interior intersection is transverse and consists of finitely many embedded circles and properly ending embedded arcs, whose endpoints lie only on $L$, with a fixed boundary collar arrangement already supplied. Then an ambient isotopy of $F_+$ fixed near $L$ removes all interior circle components of its intersection with the original comparison surface $F_-$, while retaining its arc components and the boundary collar arrangement. Its full positive definite pairing is transported by the isotopy. The finite construction strictly reduces the circle count at each stage. The ambient isotopy need not fix the comparison surface pointwise; that surface is retained at its original position when intersections are measured.

Assume full AC. Let $F_0,F_1\subset S^3$ be compact smooth embedded surfaces with the same nonempty oriented boundary link $L$, no closed surface components, and supplied radial collars of $L$. Suppose their entire intersection is $L$ together with $n$ disjoint isolated smooth arcs with distinct endpoints on $L$. Each arc is the radial extension of a proper transverse common arc in the link exterior; its two transverse boundary-curve crossings have equal ordered signs on the boundary tori oriented outward toward the exterior. No intersection circles occur. Suppose $c(F_0)=c(F_1)=p$ and $n=\operatorname{rank}H_1(F_0;\mathbb Z)+\operatorname{rank}H_1(F_1;\mathbb Z)$.

There are $p$ disjoint smooth embedded two-spheres and a regular oriented diagram on each, connected as a graph, with exactly $n$ crossings in total, whose simultaneous small-height realization is smoothly ambient isotopic to the original $L$. Every sphere carries a nonempty group of complete link components. The induced coloring by the two original surfaces gives checkerboard surfaces, made of one disk in each region of a color and a half-twisted band at each crossing, in the smooth ambient-isotopy classes of $F_0$ and $F_1$, with their boundary orientations transported. In particular, if $L$ is nonsplit, then $p=1$ and the construction gives a connected regular oriented diagram of $L$ on a single projection sphere. If the full normal-transfer pairings on the original surfaces are definite with opposite signs, all the resulting diagrams are alternating. No primeness assumption is used, so this conclusion includes composite nonsplit links.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$. For each $p\in M$, let
$\gamma_p:I_p\to M$ be the maximal integral curve through $p$, and set

$$ \mathcal D:=\{(t,p)\in\mathbb R\times M:t\in I_p\}, \qquad \Phi(t,p):=\gamma_p(t). $$

Then $\mathcal D$ is open in $\mathbb R\times M$, each fibre $\mathcal D_p$ is
an interval containing $0$, the map $\Phi:\mathcal D\to M$ is smooth, and
$\Phi$ is the unique maximal local flow generated by $X$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $W$ be a compact smooth $1$-manifold, possibly with boundary (the empty manifold included). Then $W$ is diffeomorphic to a finite disjoint union of copies of the circle $S^1$ and of the closed interval $[0,1]$. Consequently the boundary $\partial W$ is a finite set of even cardinality: every circle component contributes no boundary point and every interval component contributes exactly two, so $\#\partial W$ is twice the number of interval components of $W$. The classification neither assumes orientability nor compactness of the connected model; compactness is used only to finish with finitely many circles and closed intervals.

derivations.claim: Apply [F1] and retain the exact radial collars on smaller tubes. Both original homology groups and pairings are unchanged under that smooth isotopy. By [F2] their component counts agree; call the common positive integer $p$. Remove still smaller open tubes of $L$ to form a compact exterior $X$. The two surface boundaries on its tori are already transverse and their entire intersections in a collar of those tori are the radial segments at the finitely many boundary crossings. These segments are transverse to the tori and to each other as surface intersections.

Make the surfaces transverse on the rest of $X$ without changing these collars. In $S^3\setminus L$ the comparison $F_-\setminus L$ is closed and boundaryless. Cover the compact possible intersection region away from smaller fixed collars by finitely many ambient coordinate balls, and choose bump-supported coordinate frame fields spanning the ambient tangent spaces on smaller balls. Compose their short time-$a_j$ flows. At parameter zero the evaluation on $F_+\setminus L$ is a submersion at every possible nontransverse intersection in that compact region; the same holds for sufficiently small parameters by compactness and nonzero minors. On the remaining fixed collar the evaluation is already transverse, and away from the possible intersection region compact separation excludes new intersections. Hence the total family is transverse everywhere. By [F5] choose an arbitrarily small transverse parameter and use its flow path as the ambient isotopy. Its support misses the fixed collars. The transverse intersection in $X$ is a compact smooth one-manifold with boundary exactly the prescribed torus crossings: the implicit-function coordinates from [F5] give its local line charts, and the exact radial collar charts give its boundary half-line charts. By [F6] it is a finite disjoint union of circles and proper embedded arcs.

Apply [F3] to remove the interior circles, retaining all these arcs and the smaller boundary collars. Extend every proper arc radially through its two collar segments to $L$. It remains a smooth embedded arc, because near the exterior tori it was already radial; the distinct torus intersections have distinct base parameters and hence distinct endpoints on $L$. The finite disjoint family has mutually disjoint isolated neighborhoods by compactness. Both endpoints have the same ordered sign by [F1], even when they lie on different boundary tori, since all those tori have the specified outward orientation and all the ordered crossings have that common sign. Consequently every extended arc is standard in the precise hypothesis of [F4]. No other intersection occurs besides these arcs and $L$.

Each arc contributes two torus endpoints and no circle remains. Thus its number is $n=\frac12\sum_i d_i=b_1(F_+)+b_1(F_-)$ by [F1]. The surfaces still have their original component counts and homology ranks because every operation was an ambient isotopy of the changed surface. We have therefore verified all hypotheses of [F4], including the numerical balance, equal component counts, supplied radial collars, distinct endpoints and isolated standard arcs. Apply that reconstruction. It supplies exactly $p$ smooth sphere diagrams of the original smooth link with $n$ crossings in total, transporting the individual checkerboard-surface classes; their pairings are opposite definite, so every diagram is alternating.

Since the original link is nonsplit, [F4] forces $p=1$. Hence both original surfaces are connected and the output is one connected alternating diagram with the asserted crossing count. Compose the finitely many smooth isotopies in the normalization, perturbation, circle removal and reconstruction to recover each original smooth surface class, retaining the boundary orientations. All component and crossing assertions therefore refer to the original supplied pair. This argument used nonsplitting and never primeness, so it retains composite nonsplit links without importing a knot-only prime-decomposition theorem or a flyping assertion.
